passages.title: The Return of the Urban Tram
passages.text:
Between 1900 and 1930, the electric tram was the ordinary way to cross a European or North American city. Rails ran down the middle of the main streets, cars arrived every few minutes, and fares were low enough that clerks and factory workers used them daily. Within four decades most of those systems had been torn up. The story of why they vanished, and why many cities are now laying rails again, says a great deal about how transport decisions are actually made.

The usual explanation is that the private car simply won. Cars were faster door to door, they carried families and shopping, and as incomes rose after 1945 more households could afford one. There is obvious truth in this. But the timing does not fit neatly. In several cities the tram network was closed years before car ownership became widespread, and the decision was taken by municipal committees rather than by passengers drifting away. Ridership on some closed lines was still rising when the closure was announced.

A second factor was the condition of the infrastructure itself. Tram track is expensive to maintain. Rails set into a road surface wear at a different rate from the asphalt around them, and by the late 1930s much of the network laid before the First World War was reaching the end of its life. Wartime shortages postponed the reckoning; when it arrived, councils faced a large bill for renewal at exactly the moment when buses were being marketed as a flexible, cheap alternative that required no track at all. A bus route could be moved with a signpost. To a committee looking at a deficit, that argument was difficult to refuse.

What the committees did not price was the cost of the switch to everyone else. Buses shared road space with the growing volume of cars, so they were subject to the same congestion. As journeys became slower and less predictable, passengers who had a choice moved to their own vehicles, which added to the congestion that had slowed the buses in the first place. Several transport historians describe this as a ratchet: each turn made the next turn easier, and none of them was easy to reverse.

The return of the tram, from the 1980s onward, was not driven by nostalgia. It began in cities that had run out of road. Once a corridor is full, adding a lane usually fills again within a few years, a pattern documented often enough to have its own name, induced demand. A tram lane carries far more people per metre of street width than a general traffic lane, and it does so predictably, because it is separated from the cars. Predictability turns out to matter more to passengers than raw speed: a service that is reliably slow is easier to plan around than one that is sometimes fast.

Modern systems also learned from the old ones. Where the pre-war tram stopped every two hundred metres, the modern equivalent often stops every five hundred, which raises average speed considerably at a modest cost in walking distance. Low floors, level boarding and off-vehicle ticketing cut the time spent standing still at each stop, which on a busy line can account for a third of the journey. None of these are dramatic innovations. Together they change the economics.

The rebuilding is not universally successful. A tram line is a fixed asset in a way a bus route is not, and if it is built along the wrong corridor the mistake is permanent and visible. Construction disrupts the businesses along the route for a year or more, and some never recover. Costs frequently exceed the original estimate, sometimes substantially, and the schemes that overrun are the ones that get written about. Cities that have done it well tend to share an unglamorous characteristic: they decided the route on the basis of where people already travelled, rather than where planners hoped development would follow.

That last point is the connection between the two eras. The systems torn up in the 1950s were dismantled by people who believed they were reading the future correctly, and who were working with the costs that appeared on their own balance sheet. The costs that did not appear there arrived anyway, and were paid by somebody else, over a longer period. Whether the current generation of schemes is making a symmetrical error is not something that can be settled now.

passages.title: Reading the Rings of Trees
passages.text:
In temperate climates a tree adds one layer of wood each year, and the layers are visible in cross-section as rings. Wide rings correspond to favourable growing seasons and narrow rings to poor ones. Because every tree in a region experiences the same weather, trees of the same species growing near one another produce the same pattern of wide and narrow rings. That shared pattern is what makes the rings useful as a record. A single tree tells you about one organism; a pattern repeated across many trees tells you about a climate.

The technique that exploits this is called crossdating. An investigator measures the ring widths of a living tree whose outer ring corresponds to a known year, then looks for the same sequence of wide and narrow rings in a beam taken from an older structure. Where the sequences overlap, the beam can be dated exactly. The overlapping beam then extends the reference sequence further back, and the process repeats. Chronologies assembled in this way now reach back more than eight thousand years in some regions, and each year in them is a calendar year rather than an estimate.

The precision is the point. Radiocarbon dating, the other main technique available to archaeologists, returns a range rather than a date, and the width of that range is rarely less than several decades. For many questions a range is sufficient. For others it is not. If the question is whether a particular roof beam was cut before or after a documented siege, a range that spans the siege answers nothing. Tree rings, where the wood survives, can settle it.

The method has strict limits, and they are worth stating plainly. It requires a species that produces one clear ring per year, which excludes most tropical trees, where growth is not interrupted by a cold season. It requires enough rings in the sample to produce a distinctive pattern; a beam with thirty rings may match the reference sequence in several places by chance. It requires that the outermost ring be present, or the date obtained is the date of some year before felling rather than the felling itself, and carpenters routinely trimmed away the outer wood. A date reported without this qualification can be wrong by decades in a direction that is not random: always too early.

Beyond dating, the rings carry environmental information. A ring formed during a drought is narrow, and a sequence of narrow rings across many trees over a wide area indicates a regional drought rather than a local misfortune. Reconstructions built this way have identified severe multi-year droughts in the American Southwest that coincide with the abandonment of settlements, and comparable episodes elsewhere. The correspondence is suggestive, and it has often been reported as though it settled the matter. It does not. A drought that coincides with an abandonment establishes that the two happened together; it does not establish that people left because of it, and the archaeological record in several of these cases shows movement beginning before the drought did.

Rings also record events other than weather. A frost severe enough to damage growing cells leaves a distinctive damaged layer, and such frost rings appear in the same year across widely separated regions after some large volcanic eruptions, which inject material into the upper atmosphere and cool the surface. Because the ring gives an exact year, these layers have been used to date eruptions whose historical records are vague or contradictory. Scars from fire are preserved in the same way, and a fire history assembled from scarred trees can show how frequently a particular forest burned before modern suppression policies began.

None of this makes the rings a transparent window. Interpretation involves judgement about which trees to sample, how to combine sequences that disagree, and how to separate the effects of climate from the effects of a tree's own ageing, since rings tend to narrow as a trunk widens regardless of conditions: the same annual increment of wood is spread over a longer circumference. Different laboratories processing the same raw measurements have produced reconstructions that differ in their details. What the rings offer is not certainty but an unusually well-anchored starting point: a set of dates that are exact, from which the arguments can proceed.

passages.title: Why Buildings Fall Down Less Often
passages.topic: structural engineering and the sharing of failure
passages.text:
Large buildings collapse far less often than they did a century ago, and the reason is not that engineers have become cleverer. It is that the profession developed a systematic habit of studying its own failures, and of treating each one as information that belonged to everybody rather than as an embarrassment belonging to one firm.

The habit was not adopted willingly. Through most of the nineteenth century, a structural failure was handled as a private matter between the builder, the client and, if anyone had died, the courts. Detailed findings rarely circulated. An engineer in Glasgow might repeat, in 1880, an error that had already killed people in Manchester in 1868, simply because nobody had told him about it.

What changed the pattern was a series of disasters too public to be handled quietly. The collapse of the Tay Bridge in 1879, which took a train and its passengers into the river below, produced an inquiry whose findings were printed and argued over across Europe. The inquiry concluded that the bridge had been designed without adequate allowance for wind pressure — a factor its designer had considered, but had estimated at roughly a fifth of what later measurement suggested. The importance of the case was less the specific error than the precedent: the reasoning behind a failure had been laid out in public for other engineers to read.

From that beginning, a body of shared knowledge accumulated, and much of it took a form that is easy to overlook. Building codes are often described as bureaucratic obstacles, and in their day-to-day operation they can certainly feel that way. But a code is, in substance, a record of past failures written in the form of instructions. A clause specifying a minimum thickness, or a maximum span, or a required margin above the calculated load, is usually there because at some point a structure built to a lesser standard came down.

This gives codes a characteristic that is genuinely awkward. They are conservative by design, and they accumulate rather than simplify. Each generation adds its lessons, and few clauses are ever removed, because removing one requires proving a negative — that the failure it prevents can no longer occur. The result is a document that grows steadily more cautious and more complex, and that occasionally forbids things which modern materials would handle perfectly well.

There is a second and less comfortable pattern. Failures cluster around novelty. Structures built in a familiar way, using familiar materials, at familiar scales, almost never fail; the accumulated caution covers them. Failures happen at the edges — when a span is longer than any previously attempted, when a material is used in a role it has not filled before, or when a form is copied from one climate into another. In each case the code has nothing to say, because nothing has yet gone wrong in that particular way.

Engineers are aware of this, and the standard response is to add margin where the calculations are least certain. But margin is expensive, and the pressure to reduce it is constant and comes from people who are not being unreasonable. A client who is told that a design carries a safety factor of three will quite naturally ask what would be lost by using two and a half. The honest answer is often that nobody knows precisely — which is an uncomfortable thing to say and a difficult thing to charge for.

The most instructive modern cases are therefore not the collapses but the near-misses: structures where an error was found before it caused harm. The best known is a New York tower whose engineer, prompted by a student's question, rechecked his own calculations and discovered that the building as built was vulnerable to winds striking it at the corners rather than the faces. The repairs were carried out quietly, at night, over several months. The case is now taught widely, though it should be noted that it became public only years afterwards, and that the incentives at the time pointed strongly towards silence.

That last point is where the story remains unfinished. The discipline's improvement rests on failures being examined and shared, and the pressures against sharing — legal, commercial, reputational — have not weakened. What has changed is that most engineers now regard concealment as professionally disgraceful rather than merely risky. Whether that norm holds when it is expensive to honour is tested somewhere every year.

passages.title: The Problem of Measuring Poverty
passages.text:
Few statistics are quoted as confidently as the number of people living in poverty, and few rest on foundations as contested. The difficulty is not that the data are poor, though in many countries they are. It is that the question being answered changes depending on how poverty is defined, and there is no definition that is simply correct.

The oldest approach is absolute. It sets a threshold based on what a person needs to survive — typically a basket of food sufficient for a given calorie intake, plus an allowance for shelter and other necessities — and counts everyone below it. Its appeal is obvious: it produces a line that can be compared across countries and across decades, and it makes claims about progress possible. Most headline figures showing large falls in global poverty since 1990 rest on a threshold of this kind.

The objections to it are equally clear. A basket of goods adequate in one place may be useless in another; a calorie requirement says nothing about whether a person can travel to work, or heat a home in a cold climate. And because the threshold must be converted between currencies, the resulting figure is sensitive to the exchange rates used. Revisions to those conversion factors have, on more than one occasion, moved the estimated number of people in poverty by tens of millions without anyone's circumstances having changed at all.

The alternative is relative. Here poverty is defined by distance from the middle of one's own society — commonly, a household income below some fraction of the national median. This captures something the absolute approach misses: that being poor is partly about exclusion from the ordinary life of the place where one lives, and that a person who cannot afford what everyone around them takes for granted is meaningfully deprived, whatever their calorie intake.

But the relative measure has a property that troubles many people when they first encounter it. Because it moves with the median, it can register changes that feel wrong. If a recession reduces middle incomes while the poorest are protected by transfers, measured relative poverty falls — not because anybody has become better off, but because the line itself has dropped. Conversely, a period of broad prosperity can raise measured poverty even as the poorest gain in real terms.

A third approach abandons income altogether. Multidimensional measures count deprivations directly: whether a household has clean water, whether its children attend school, whether anyone in it is malnourished, whether the dwelling has a floor. A household is counted as poor if it is deprived on enough dimensions at once. This has the advantage of describing conditions rather than proxies, and it can identify households that an income measure would miss — those with some cash income but no access to services.

Its weakness is that the choice of dimensions, and of how to weight them against each other, is unavoidably a judgement. Deciding that a lack of electricity counts for as much as a child out of school is not a finding; it is a decision, and reasonable people make it differently. The measure's designers are generally candid about this, but the candour rarely survives the journey into a newspaper headline.

None of the three is a fraud, and none is complete. What matters practically is that they are not interchangeable, and that they can move in opposite directions over the same period in the same country. Absolute poverty can fall while relative poverty rises; multidimensional poverty can improve while both income measures worsen, if services expand during a downturn.

There is also a practical asymmetry between the three that is rarely mentioned. Absolute and relative measures can be produced from household income surveys that many countries already run, at modest additional cost. Multidimensional measures require asking about a dozen separate conditions, household by household, which is slower and considerably more expensive. Where budgets are tight, the measure chosen is therefore sometimes the one that is affordable rather than the one that is most informative — and that constraint bears hardest on exactly the countries where the question matters most.

This has a consequence for anyone reading such figures. The useful question is not "how many people are poor", which cannot be answered without a prior choice, but "which measure is being used, and what does it treat as important". A claim that poverty has fallen is, on its own, close to uninformative. It becomes informative only when the definition is stated — and the definition is precisely the part that headlines omit.

passages.title: Why Some Lakes Turn Over
passages.text:
A deep lake in a temperate climate is not a single body of water. For much of the year it is layered, and the layers barely mix. Understanding why they form, and what happens when they break down, explains a great deal about where fish can live and why some lakes suffocate in summer.

The layering is a consequence of an unusual property of water: its density does not increase steadily as it cools. Water is densest at about four degrees Celsius, and becomes less dense both above and below that temperature. This is why ice floats, and it is also why a lake in midsummer is arranged the way it is.

By July, the sun has warmed the upper metres considerably. That warm water is less dense than the cold water below it, so it sits on top and stays there. Between the warm surface layer and the cold deep water lies a narrow zone in which temperature drops sharply — sometimes ten degrees within a metre or two. This zone acts as a barrier. Wind can stir the surface layer thoroughly, but it rarely has the energy to push warm water down through the barrier or draw cold water up.

The consequences for the deep water are considerable. Cut off from the surface, it receives no new oxygen from the atmosphere. Meanwhile, organic material — dead algae, mostly — sinks continuously from above and decomposes, and decomposition consumes oxygen. In a lake with abundant nutrients, and therefore abundant algae, the deep water can be stripped of oxygen entirely by late summer. Fish that require cold water are then caught in an unpleasant squeeze: the surface is too warm for them and the depths have no oxygen. In some lakes the habitable band narrows to a few metres.

Then, in autumn, the arrangement collapses. As air temperatures fall, the surface layer cools. Once it reaches the temperature of the water below, the density difference vanishes, the barrier disappears, and a moderate wind is sufficient to mix the entire lake from top to bottom. This event is called turnover, and it happens over a matter of days.

Turnover recharges the deep water with oxygen, which is essential to the lake's recovery. But it also lifts nutrients that had accumulated at the bottom back into the sunlit upper layers, and that can trigger a burst of algal growth in autumn. In lakes that receive heavy fertiliser runoff, turnover can produce an algal bloom that is visible from shore within a week.

Most temperate lakes turn over twice a year: once in autumn as described, and once in spring, when ice melts and the surface warms towards four degrees before summer layering re-establishes itself. Lakes that mix twice annually are called dimictic, and the pattern is common enough that it was long treated as the standard case in textbooks.

It is not, however, universal, and the exceptions are informative. Very deep tropical lakes may not mix at all: without a cold season the surface never cools enough to erase the density difference, and their depths can remain oxygen-free and undisturbed for centuries. Shallow lakes, at the other extreme, may mix continuously all summer, because wind reaches the bottom and no stable layering can establish itself.

The distinction matters for anyone managing a lake. A reservoir that supplies drinking water is usually drawn from the depths, and water taken from an oxygen-free layer carries dissolved iron and manganese that must be removed before use. Managers of such reservoirs sometimes install aerators to break the layering artificially, at considerable running cost, precisely to avoid treating water that the lake's own physics has degraded.

There is a further point that has become important recently. Because the whole mechanism depends on the surface cooling to meet the deep water, warmer winters lengthen the period of layering. Several long-monitored lakes now stratify earlier in spring and turn over later in autumn than they did fifty years ago, which extends the season during which their depths are without oxygen. The lakes have not become warmer in any simple sense — the deep water is often unchanged. What has changed is the length of time it spends sealed off.

passages.title: Why Planting Mangroves So Often Fails
passages.text:
Along tropical coastlines, mangrove forests grow in the difficult zone between land and sea, flooded twice a day by salt water that would kill most trees. For decades they were treated as wasteland: drained for fish ponds, cut for charcoal, cleared for harbours. That view has now reversed. Governments that once paid to remove mangroves pledge to restore them, and the targets are announced in millions of trees. The pledges are easy to make. Keeping them has proved far harder, and the reasons are worth understanding.

The case for restoration begins with waves. A mangrove forest weakens a wave by friction: every root, trunk and branch that the water must push past takes a share of its energy. Field measurements show that a wave can lose most of its height within the first hundred metres of forest. What matters is therefore not the height of the trees but the width of the belt. A strip of forest a few metres deep is decoration; a belt several hundred metres deep is infrastructure, and villages behind such belts have repeatedly recorded less flooding than their neighbours during the same storms.

Protection is not the only service. The tangle of roots shelters juvenile fish and crabs until they are large enough to survive open water, which is why fishing communities often notice their catches falling years after a nearby forest is cleared. The mud matters too. Because it is waterlogged and poor in oxygen, dead plant material rots very slowly, so carbon accumulates in the soil for centuries. Hectare for hectare, mangrove soils typically hold several times more carbon than the soils of forests inland. Both services disappear quietly when the trees do, and both are costly to replace once they are gone.

Enthusiasm has produced planting campaigns on an impressive scale. Volunteers and schoolchildren have set millions of seedlings into coastal mud, sometimes hundreds of thousands in a single day, and each seedling costs very little to buy. The results have been sobering. Teams who returned to survey the sites years later found that in many large campaigns fewer than one seedling in five had survived, and that at some sites none had.

The reason is rarely the seedlings themselves. Campaigns favour one or two species whose large seeds are easy to collect and handle, whether or not those species suit the site. More damaging still is the choice of ground. Seedlings are typically planted on open mudflats in front of the existing shore, because the space is empty and no one must be asked for land. But those flats are empty for a reason: they sit too low in the tidal range, so young trees are submerged for longer each day than they can tolerate. A forest is being demanded from ground that mangroves never colonised on their own.

An alternative approach starts with water rather than trees. In many failed sites, the original forest died because embankments and abandoned ponds had blocked the daily movement of the tide. Where engineers reopen the old channels and let the sea flow in and out again, mangrove seeds float in on their own, settle where conditions suit them, and grow. Surveys of such sites report survival far higher than in planting campaigns. The method's weakness is presentational: for the first few years there is little to photograph except mud and water.

That weakness matters because of how restoration is funded. Donors and agencies must report results quickly, and the number of seedlings planted is available on the day of the event, complete with photographs of volunteers at work. The number of trees still alive after five years arrives long after the budget has closed and the officials have moved on. The system rewards the number that is easy to count, and the number that is easy to count is the wrong one.

None of this means restoration is hopeless. It means the measure of success needs changing. Projects that begin by fixing the movement of water, accept whichever species arrive naturally, and commit to counting survivors for a decade have an encouraging record. They are slower, less visible and harder to summarise in a press release — which is precisely why they need defenders who understand what the photographs of planting days do not show.

explain.whyOthersFail: Kelangsungan hidup yang lebih rendah membalik isi teks; soal biaya yang lebih besar dan bibit dari daerah lain tidak pernah dinyatakan.

passages.title: What Makes Batik Batik
passages.text:
Ask a visitor what batik is and you will usually hear a description of a pattern: deep browns and indigos arranged into flowers, birds and geometric borders. The answer is understandable, and it is wrong in a way that matters. Batik is not a pattern but a process. A cloth is batik because its design was built up by repeatedly drawing hot wax onto the fabric and dyeing whatever the wax left exposed. A printed cloth that copies a batik motif, however faithfully, is not batik at all — and the difference, far from being a technicality, decides who earns a living from the word.

The process is a long negotiation with wax. A maker heats a blend of waxes until it flows, then lays it down wherever the cloth must stay undyed. When the cloth is dipped, the dye claims only the bare fibre. The wax is then boiled away, new lines are drawn, and the cloth is dyed again; each cycle adds a single colour, so a design in four colours means the entire sequence performed four times. Mistakes cannot be corrected, only incorporated into the design.

The wax itself is engineered. Makers blend paraffin, beeswax and tree resins, and it is the proportions of the blend that decide how the coating behaves in the dye bath: more paraffin leaves it brittle, so that dye seeps into hairline cracks and produces the fine veining prized in some traditions; more beeswax keeps the drawn line supple and clean. The dyes were historically botanical — indigo leaves for the blues, soga bark for the warm browns — and demanded days of repeated dipping for a single colour. The arrival of synthetic dyes in the late nineteenth century collapsed those days into hours and rewrote the economics of every workshop.

Within the craft there are two instruments. The canting, a small copper kettle with a spout, is held like a pen; a cloth drawn with it — batik tulis — can occupy a maker for weeks or months. The cap, a copper stamp, presses the same waxed design onto the cloth in seconds, and a stamped piece can be finished in days. Purists rank the first far above the second, but both are batik, because in both the pattern exists as wax before it exists as colour. The meaningful boundary lies elsewhere: a textile printed with a batik design involves no wax at all, and no resistance for the dye to negotiate.

The boundary matters because the imitation is cheap. A printed copy sells for a fraction of the price of the cloth it mimics, and to a hurried eye in a market the two are difficult to tell apart. Workshops that pay for weeks of skilled labour are undercut by factories that pay for none, and the price a genuine cloth can command is dragged down by objects that merely resemble it.

The cloth itself offers a defence, for those who know where to look. Because hot wax soaks through the fabric, a genuine batik carries its design almost equally on both faces; on a printed imitation the reverse side is noticeably paler, a ghost of the front. Hand-waxed lines also hesitate — they thicken where the maker paused and thin where the hand moved quickly — while printed lines are inhumanly even. On newer cloth there is often a plainer signature: a faint smell of wax that no printing press leaves behind.

In 2009, UNESCO added Indonesian batik to its list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity. The listing raised the craft's public standing: offices adopted batik Fridays, demand rose, and the word acquired a patriotic glow. The irony is that much of the new demand has been met by printed cloth, so that a decision honouring a technique has chiefly enlarged the market for its imitation.

Meanwhile the technique rests on labour that is largely invisible. Most of the waxing is done by women, paid by the piece at rates that reward speed over the patience the work demands, and many of them are past middle age. The skill takes years to acquire, and young workers who calculate what those years will pay are choosing other trades. A tradition can survive bad publicity; it cannot survive the retirement of everyone who practises it.

What deserves protection, then, is not a set of motifs, which can be photographed and reproduced endlessly, but the knowledge held in hands — the feel for wax at the right temperature, for a line drawn at the right speed. Protecting that requires the unglamorous machinery of definition: a rule that reserves the word batik for wax-resist cloth, honest labelling for everything else, and prices that make the years of apprenticeship worth a young worker's while.

questions.stem: Lengkapi ringkasan — pilih kata/frasa dari teks yang mengisi bagian kosong: "According to the writer, a cloth only qualifies as batik if its design was made with ______ before any dye touched the fabric."

explain.evidence: A cloth is batik because its design was built up by repeatedly drawing hot wax onto the fabric
explain.why: Definisi penulis berpusat pada lilin: desain harus lahir sebagai lilin sebelum lahir sebagai warna. Canting maupun cap sama-sama sah karena keduanya memakai lilin.
explain.whyOthersFail: 'A copper stamp' hanya salah satu alat (cap) - batik tulis tidak memakainya; 'indigo' adalah pewarna, bukan perintangnya; 'a printing press' justru penanda kain tiruan yang tanpa lilin sama sekali.

questions.stem: Lengkapi ringkasan — pilih kata/frasa dari teks yang mengisi bagian kosong: "How the wax coating behaves in the dye bath depends on the ______ of the blend."

explain.evidence: it is the proportions of the blend that decide how the coating behaves in the dye bath
explain.why: Teks menyebutnya eksplisit: perbandingan campuran parafin, lilin lebah, dan damar yang menentukan - lebih banyak parafin membuat lapisan getas dan retak halus, lebih banyak lilin lebah membuat garis lentur.
explain.whyOthersFail: Suhu ('temperature') memang disebut, tetapi untuk melelehkan lilin agar mengalir saat digambar - bukan penentu perilakunya di bak celup. Warna adalah hasil pencelupan, bukan sifat campuran; harga campuran tidak dibahas sama sekali.

questions.stem: Lengkapi ringkasan — pilih kata/frasa dari teks yang mengisi bagian kosong: "Finishing a cloth drawn with the canting can take weeks or even ______, whereas a stamped piece takes days."

explain.evidence: a cloth drawn with it — batik tulis — can occupy a maker for weeks or months
explain.why: Teks menyandingkan dua durasi: batik tulis memakan waktu berminggu-minggu sampai berbulan-bulan, batik cap selesai dalam hitungan hari.
explain.whyOthersFail: 'Seconds' adalah waktu cap menekankan pola sekali tekan, bukan durasi menyelesaikan kain; 'hours' adalah efek pewarna sintetis pada pencelupan; 'years' dipakai teks untuk lama menguasai keterampilan, bukan lama membuat satu kain.

questions.stem: Lengkapi ringkasan — pilih kata/frasa dari teks yang mengisi bagian kosong: "A quick test of authenticity: on a printed copy, the pattern viewed from the ______ of the cloth looks much fainter."

explain.evidence: on a printed imitation the reverse side is noticeably paler, a ghost of the front
explain.why: Karena lilin panas meresap menembus kain, batik asli membawa desain hampir sama jelas di kedua muka; tiruan cetak hanya kuat di muka depan sehingga sisi baliknya pucat.
explain.whyOthersFail: 'Front' membalik faktanya - sisi depan tiruan justru yang jelas; 'borders' hanya bagian motif dan 'fibre' hanya serat yang diwarnai - keduanya tidak pernah dijadikan penanda keaslian oleh teks.

questions.stem: Lengkapi ringkasan — pilih kata/frasa dari teks yang mengisi bagian kosong: "Much of the demand created by the 2009 listing has in fact been supplied by ______ cloth."

explain.evidence: much of the new demand has been met by printed cloth
explain.why: Inilah ironi yang ditunjuk penulis: keputusan yang menghormati sebuah teknik justru memperbesar pasar bagi tiruannya yang dicetak tanpa lilin.
explain.whyOthersFail: 'Genuine', 'stamped', dan 'waxed' semuanya menunjuk kain yang benar-benar memakai lilin - justru kebalikan dari yang menampung lonjakan permintaan menurut teks.

questions.stem: Lengkapi ringkasan — pilih kata/frasa dari teks yang mengisi bagian kosong: "The writer concludes that protection requires reserving the word batik for ______ cloth."

explain.evidence: a rule that reserves the word batik for wax-resist cloth
explain.why: Penutupnya konkret: aturan yang mengunci kata 'batik' hanya untuk kain perintang lilin, pelabelan jujur untuk selainnya, dan harga yang membuat tahun-tahun magang sepadan.
explain.whyOthersFail: 'Printed' justru kain yang HARUS dilabeli sebagai bukan batik; 'patriotic' hanya menggambarkan citra kata itu setelah 2009; 'photographed' dipakai teks untuk motif yang bisa ditiru tanpa batas.

questions.stem: Paragraf mana yang menjelaskan cara mengenali batik asli dari kainnya sendiri?

explain.evidence: a genuine batik carries its design almost equally on both faces
explain.why: Paragraf 6 memberi tiga penanda pada kainnya: sisi balik yang sama jelas, garis tangan yang menebal-menipis, dan bau lilin yang samar.
explain.whyOthersFail: Paragraf 4 membedakan canting dan cap; paragraf 5 soal harga tiruan; paragraf 7 soal pengakuan UNESCO.

questions.stem: Paragraf mana yang menjelaskan mengapa harga batik asli ikut tertekan?

explain.evidence: the price a genuine cloth can command is dragged down by objects that merely resemble it
explain.why: Paragraf 5 memaparkan mekanismenya: tiruan cetak dijual sepersekian harga, mata yang terburu-buru sulit membedakan, dan bengkel yang membayar tenaga terampil kalah bersaing.
explain.whyOthersFail: Paragraf 3 soal kimia lilin dan pewarna; paragraf 7 soal dampak pengakuan UNESCO; paragraf 9 kesimpulan tentang apa yang layak dilindungi.

questions.stem: Paragraf mana yang membahas siapa yang mengerjakan pemalaman dan bagaimana mereka dibayar?

explain.evidence: Most of the waxing is done by women, paid by the piece at rates that reward speed over the patience the work demands
explain.why: Paragraf 8 membuka sisi tenaga kerja yang nyaris tak terlihat: sebagian besar perempuan, dibayar borongan, dan generasi muda memilih pekerjaan lain.
explain.whyOthersFail: Paragraf 5 soal persaingan harga, paragraf 6 soal cara mengenali kain asli, paragraf 7 soal UNESCO - tak satu pun membahas upah perajin.

questions.stem: The writer believes a printed cloth with a batik motif deserves to be called batik.

explain.evidence: A printed cloth that copies a batik motif, however faithfully, is not batik at all
explain.why: Pandangan penulis dinyatakan tegas di paragraf pembuka: sesetia apa pun tiruannya, kain cetak bukan batik. Jawabannya No.
explain.whyOthersFail: Yes membalik pendirian penulis. Not Given salah karena ini justru tesis utama tulisannya - YNNG menguji PANDANGAN penulis, dan di sini pandangannya eksplisit.

questions.stem: The writer sees an irony in what followed the UNESCO listing.

explain.evidence: The irony is that much of the new demand has been met by printed cloth
explain.why: Penulis memakai kata 'irony' sendiri: pengakuan atas sebuah teknik justru memperbesar pasar tiruan yang meninggalkan teknik itu.
explain.whyOthersFail: No membalik sikap penulis; Not Given salah karena kalimatnya ada, lengkap dengan penilaiannya.

questions.stem: The writer believes synthetic dyes made batik less beautiful than natural dyes did.

explain.evidence: The arrival of synthetic dyes in the late nineteenth century collapsed those days into hours and rewrote the economics of every workshop
explain.why: Yang dinilai penulis hanyalah dampak WAKTU dan EKONOMI pewarna sintetis. Soal mana yang lebih indah, teksnya diam sama sekali - jadi Not Given.
explain.whyOthersFail: Yes menambahkan penilaian estetika yang tidak pernah ditulis; No juga salah karena penulis tidak membela pewarna sintetis - ia sekadar tidak berpendapat. Not Given berarti penulisnya diam, bukan pernyataannya terdengar salah.

questions.stem: The writer thinks stamped batik should not count as real batik.

explain.evidence: both are batik, because in both the pattern exists as wax before it exists as colour
explain.why: Penulis justru membela batik cap: kaum puris boleh menempatkan tulis di atas cap, tetapi keduanya batik karena polanya lahir sebagai lilin. Jawabannya No.

passages.title: Chemosynthesis and the Rewriting of the Deep Sea
passages.topic: deep-sea biology and the limits of observation
passages.text:
Until the late 1970s, the deep ocean floor was regarded as a biological near-desert, and the presumption seemed unassailable. Sunlight is extinguished within a few hundred meters of the surface, and every food web then known rested ultimately on photosynthesis. Whatever lived in the abyss was assumed to subsist on marine snow — the sparse, slow descent of organic particles from the sunlit layers above — a ration so meagre that scarcity appeared to be the deep sea's defining condition, and its fauna a thin scattering of scavengers adapted to permanent shortage.

That presumption did not survive the descent of a research submersible to a volcanic ridge in the eastern Pacific in 1977. Around fissures where seawater, having percolated through hot rock, re-emerged laden with dissolved minerals, the observers found not scarcity but profusion: beds of clams, thickets of tubeworms up to two meters long, and crabs and fish in densities exceeding those of the surrounding seafloor by orders of magnitude. The water sustaining this crowd was far warmer than the near-freezing abyss around it, and it carried compounds that, by every textbook then in print, should have made the neighborhood poisonous rather than fertile.

The explanation overturned a century of assumptions about where the energy for life must come from. Bacteria at these vents oxidize the hydrogen sulfide dissolved in the venting fluid and use the energy released to fix carbon — chemosynthesis, a metabolism whose primary energy source is chemical rather than solar. The giant tubeworms proved to have neither mouth nor gut; they are, in effect, housing for symbiotic bacteria, which occupy an internal organ evolved for that purpose and provision their host from within. The independence from sunlight is nonetheless partial rather than absolute: the oxidation on which the whole edifice depends consumes oxygen, and the ocean's oxygen is overwhelmingly the product of photosynthesis conducted elsewhere.

The ecology that results is shaped by impermanence. An individual vent field may remain active for decades rather than millennia; when the flow ceases, the community it sustained starves. Persistence therefore depends on dispersal: larvae must drift, or be carried by currents, to colonize new fields whose locations no adult will survive to reach. The faunas assembled this way are strikingly endemic — many vent species occur nowhere else — and their apparent rarity may say less about their abundance than about the handful of sites at which anyone has looked.

That qualification points to a methodological difficulty that attends all deep-sea biology. The environment can be reached only briefly, at great cost, and by instruments that disturb what they examine. Sampling gear crushes what it collects, and a submersible announces itself with noise and displaced water long before it arrives. Generalizations about vent ecosystems accordingly rest on repeated visits to a small number of accessible sites, and it would be imprudent to assume that the few sites so far described are truly representative of the many sites that remain unvisited.

The question has acquired regulatory urgency. Vent chimneys precipitate copper, zinc and gold in concentrations that mining interests find increasingly attractive, and licenses to prospect parts of the international seabed have already been granted. Assessing what extraction would destroy, however, presupposes a baseline inventory of what is there — precisely the inventory that the difficulty of access has prevented anyone from compiling. Regulators are thus asked to weigh a quantifiable commercial gain against a loss that cannot yet be stated, an asymmetry that tends, in practice, to favor the gain.

The larger lesson of 1977 may therefore be epistemological rather than zoological. The deep sea had not been empty; it had been unexamined, and the confident assertions of its barrenness were, in retrospect, statements about the reach of the era's instruments rather than about the distribution of life. Claims of absence deserve, on this reading, a standing discount: they report where we have looked, and with what, at least as faithfully as they report what exists.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 1, what was deep-sea life assumed to subsist on?
options: Dissolved minerals rising from hot rock
Organic particles sinking from the sunlit layers
Bacteria carried down by ocean currents

explain.evidence: assumed to subsist on marine snow — the sparse, slow descent of organic particles from the sunlit layers above
explain.why: Pandangan lama: satu-satunya makanan yang sampai ke dasar adalah 'marine snow', partikel organik yang turun perlahan dari lapisan bercahaya - jatah yang sangat tipis.
explain.whyOthersFail: Mineral terlarut dan panas vulkanik justru bagian dari penemuan 1977 yang MENGGUGURKAN anggapan itu; bakteri yang terbawa arus tidak pernah disebut sebagai sumber makanan.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 3, how do the giant tubeworms obtain their nutrition?
options: They filter marine snow through specialized gills
They absorb dissolved minerals directly through the skin
They are provisioned from within by symbiotic bacteria
They prey on the clams and crabs around the vents

explain.evidence: housing for symbiotic bacteria, which occupy an internal organ evolved for that purpose and provision their host from within
explain.why: Cacing tabung raksasa tidak punya mulut maupun usus; ia pada dasarnya 'rumah' bagi bakteri simbiotik yang memberinya makan dari dalam.
explain.whyOthersFail: Justru ketiadaan mulut dan usus meniadakan penyaringan dan pemangsaan; penyerapan mineral lewat kulit tidak pernah dinyatakan - mineralnya diolah bakteri, bukan diserap inangnya langsung.

questions.stem: The word "profusion" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to

explain.evidence: the observers found not scarcity but profusion
explain.why: Kata itu dipertentangkan langsung dengan 'scarcity' (kelangkaan), lalu dirinci: hamparan kerang, rumpun cacing tabung, kepadatan berkali lipat. Lawan kelangkaan adalah kelimpahan.
explain.whyOthersFail: 'Confusion' cuma mirip bunyi; 'variety' menonjolkan keragaman padahal yang ditekankan kepadatannya; 'danger' tidak berlawanan dengan 'scarcity' sama sekali.

questions.stem: All of the following are stated about vent fields and their faunas EXCEPT:
options: A field may stay active for decades rather than millennia
A community starves once the flow of fluid stops
Many vent species are found nowhere else
Vent fields are spaced evenly along every ocean ridge

explain.evidence: An individual vent field may remain active for decades rather than millennia; when the flow ceases, the community it sustained starves.
explain.why: Tiga pernyataan pertama ada di paragraf 4, termasuk 'many vent species occur nowhere else'. Sebaran ventilasi yang MERATA di setiap punggungan tidak pernah dinyatakan di mana pun.
explain.whyOthersFail: Soal EXCEPT menghukum pembaca yang berhenti begitu menemukan satu pilihan yang benar - di sini tiga pilihan memang benar, dan yang dicari justru satu-satunya yang tidak ada di teks.

questions.stem: Which sentence best expresses the essential information in: "The independence from sunlight is nonetheless partial rather than absolute: the oxidation on which the whole edifice depends consumes oxygen, and the ocean's oxygen is overwhelmingly the product of photosynthesis conducted elsewhere"?
options: Vent life uses no sunlight directly, but it depends on oxygen that photosynthesis produced
Vent communities would survive even if photosynthesis stopped everywhere
Oxygen is scarcer at the vents than anywhere else in the ocean
Photosynthesis also takes place in the water surrounding the vents

explain.evidence: the oxidation on which the whole edifice depends consumes oxygen
explain.why: Inti kalimatnya: kemerdekaan dari matahari tidak penuh, karena oksidasi yang menopang seluruh komunitas memakai oksigen - dan oksigen laut hampir seluruhnya buah fotosintesis di tempat lain.
explain.whyOthersFail: Pilihan kedua justru membalik akibatnya; kelangkaan oksigen di ventilasi tidak pernah dibandingkan; fotosintesis di air sekitar ventilasi bertentangan dengan 'conducted elsewhere'.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from paragraph 4 about the apparent rarity of vent species?
options: It has been confirmed by systematic surveys of every ridge
It shows that vent faunas are close to extinction
It may reflect how few sites have been examined rather than true scarcity
It is caused by larvae failing to reach new fields

explain.evidence: their apparent rarity may say less about their abundance than about the handful of sites at which anyone has looked
explain.why: Penulis memberi diskon pada kesan 'langka': kesan itu mungkin lebih menceritakan sedikitnya lokasi yang pernah diperiksa daripada kelimpahan sesungguhnya.
explain.whyOthersFail: Survei sistematis setiap punggungan justru bertentangan dengan 'handful of sites'; kepunahan dan kegagalan larva tidak pernah disimpulkan - larva justru digambarkan sebagai mekanisme bertahannya.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention licenses to prospect parts of the international seabed?
options: To show that the regulatory question is no longer hypothetical
To argue that mineral concentrations have been exaggerated
To demonstrate that vent ecosystems have already been destroyed
To explain how vent chimneys precipitate metals

explain.evidence: licenses to prospect parts of the international seabed have already been granted
explain.why: Kata 'already' menunjuk fungsinya: urgensi regulasi bukan andai-andai lagi, izin pencariannya sudah keluar sementara inventaris dasarnya belum ada.
explain.whyOthersFail: Penulis tidak meragukan kadar mineralnya, tidak mengklaim ekosistemnya sudah hancur, dan proses kimianya sudah dijelaskan di kalimat sebelumnya - bukan oleh penyebutan izin.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 6, why is it difficult to assess what mining would destroy?
options: Mining technology changes faster than assessments can follow
The commercial gains have never been calculated
No baseline inventory of the ecosystems exists
Regulators lack the authority to refuse licenses

explain.evidence: presupposes a baseline inventory of what is there — precisely the inventory that the difficulty of access has prevented anyone from compiling
explain.why: Menilai kerusakan mengandaikan tahu apa yang ada di sana lebih dulu - dan justru inventaris itulah yang belum pernah bisa disusun karena sulitnya akses.
explain.whyOthersFail: Keuntungan komersial justru disebut 'quantifiable'; kecepatan teknologi tambang dan kewenangan regulator menolak izin tidak pernah dibahas.

questions.stem: A sentence has been removed from paragraph 5. Where would this sentence best fit?  "Even the light by which the animals are observed is an intrusion into a world that has never known any."  Each gap sits immediately before a labeled sentence: (A) That qualification points to a methodological difficulty that attends all deep-sea biology. (B) The environment can be reached only briefly, at great cost, and by instruments that disturb what they examine. (C) Sampling gear crushes what it collects, and a submersible announces itself with noise and displaced water long before it arrives. (D) Generalizations about vent ecosystems accordingly rest on repeated visits to a small number of accessible sites.

explain.evidence: a submersible announces itself with noise and displaced water long before it arrives...Generalizations about vent ecosystems accordingly rest
explain.why: Kata 'Even' menutup daftar gangguan yang menanjak: alat sampel merusak, kapal selam berisik, dan puncaknya - cahaya pun ikut mengganggu. Kalimat itu harus berdiri setelah daftar lengkap tersebut, di celah sebelum kesimpulan 'accordingly' pada kalimat (D).
explain.whyOthersFail: Di celah sebelum (A) dan (B) kesulitan metodologisnya bahkan belum dijabarkan; di celah sebelum (C) contoh konkretnya (alat sampel dan kapal selam) belum disebut - padahal 'Even' menutup sebuah daftar, dan daftar itu belum ada untuk ditutup.

questions.stem: What does the final paragraph suggest about claims that a region contains no life?
options: They have been abandoned entirely since 1977
They describe the limits of observation as much as the world observed
They are only ever made about the deep sea
They become reliable once instruments improve

explain.evidence: they report where we have looked, and with what, at least as faithfully as they report what exists
explain.why: Pelajaran epistemologisnya: klaim ketiadaan layak diberi 'diskon tetap' karena ia sama setianya melaporkan jangkauan instrumen kita seperti melaporkan isi dunia.
explain.whyOthersFail: Penulis meminta klaim semacam itu DIDISKON, bukan ditinggalkan sepenuhnya; ia tidak membatasinya pada laut dalam; dan instrumen yang membaik justru menegaskan bahwa klaim lama memang cerita soal alat.
